title: Who knows doesn't speak
hookLine: those who know don't speak; those who speak don't know (Tao Te Ching 56)

cards: A dinner party, and the talk turns to something everyone has a take on. One guest explains it at length. Another adds a counterpoint.
A third jumps in. Down at the end of the table sits someone who spent years working in the very field being discussed. She listens.
She asks one question. Then she passes the bread. Later, someone finds out who she was and says, why didn't you say anything?
Chapter fifty-six of the Tao Te Ching has a line about that end of the table.

teach.h: WHO KNOWS THE TAO DOESN'T RUSH TO SAY IT.
teach.b: First, the line. In James Legge's translation: "He who knows (the Tao) does not (care to) speak (about it); he who is (ever ready to) speak about it does not know it." Those parentheses are Legge's, and they matter.
In his reading, the line isn't a gag order on everyone who knows things. It's about the Tao itself, which the book's first chapter already said can't be fully named.
Talk about it too eagerly and you've shown you're holding a name, not the thing. Second, what the knower does instead.

teach.h: BLUNT THE EDGES, SOFTEN THE GLARE.
teach.b: Close the mouth and shut the doors, the chapter says; blunt the sharp edges and untangle the knots; soften the glare and become one with the dust.
The middle of those lines appears almost word for word back in chapter four.

Third, the name the chapter gives this: the mysterious agreement, or mysterious sameness. A person like this can't be won over by closeness or pushed off by distance, can't be bought or harmed, raised up or brought low.
Quiet makes them hard to move.
Fourth, the obvious question, which some readers ask: if those who know don't speak, why write a book?
The chapter doesn't answer, and the question can stay open. Closer to home, the line is a mirror for the urge to weigh in. Not every thought you hold needs to leave your mouth to be true.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter fifty-six as a teaching on restraint in speech, especially about the Tao itself, which the book's opening says can't be fully named.

games.q: what does “who knows doesn't speak” mean?
o: a rule that wise people must never speak at all
keeping secrets so that others can't learn them
the one who knows the Tao doesn't rush to talk of it

p: doesn't care to speak of it
who is ever ready to speak
lines also found in chapter four

s: in Legge's reading, the line says experts should never talk
his parentheses make it about the Tao: who knows it doesn't care to speak about it.

blunting the sharp edges, untangling the knots, softening the glare, one with the dust.

games.q: you know the Tao, and the talk at the table turns to it. what does chapter fifty-six picture you doing?
o: closing the mouth, softening the glare.
games.why: the knower in chapter fifty-six closes the mouth, blunts the edges and becomes one with the dust: the mysterious agreement.

practice: Bring to mind a conversation coming up where you'll want to weigh in, a group chat, a meeting, a family call, and find the opinion that's already loaded.
Feel the little pressure of it, the urge to be heard, and let it stay where it is, unspoken, like a stone in your pocket. Breathe around it, and notice that it's still yours even if nobody hears it.

wordCard.voice: Who knows doesn't speak. Chapter fifty-six: the one who knows the Tao doesn't rush to talk about it, and the one who's always ready to talk doesn't know it. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: the one who knows does not speak, the opening of chapter fifty-six.

carryVoice: Your line: who knows is quiet. The expert at the end of the table passed the bread. Until tomorrow.
